fr:mainmatter.fr:p: Finite-type intuitionistic predicate logic is a predicate logic over a typed term language. Thus we describe the types, then terms. The formulas over those terms will be certain terms (of type Ω), and thus mutually defined with the terms.

Given a collection of atomic type symbols \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {base}}, the collection of (all) \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {base}}-types is the smallest such that
if A ∈ \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {base}}, then A is a type
if A and B are types, A × B is a type
if A and B are types, then A → B is a type
1 is a type
either
Ω is a type, and let \mathcal {P} A ≔ A → Ω
if A is a type, \mathcal {P} A is a type, and let Ω ≔ \mathcal {P} 1
We write x : y to mean "'x' is a term of type 'y'".

Given a collection of constant term symbols \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {const}}, a collection of function symbols \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {fun}}, and a collection of relation symbols \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {rel}}, the collection of (all, possibly open) ( \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {const}} , \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {fun}} , \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {rel}} )-terms is the smallest such that
if A is a type, there are sufficient variables x : A
if (c : A) ∈ \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {const}}, then c : A
if (f~``: A₁ × … Aₙ → B") ∈ \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {fun}} and a₁ : A₁, … aₙ : Aₙ, then f(a₁, …, aₙ) : A (quotes are used to avoid making f look like a constant symbol of function type, but we don't bother to write something correct)
if R~``: A₁ × … Aₙ → Ω" ∈ \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {rel}} and a₁ : A₁, … aₙ : Aₙ, then R(a₁, …, aₙ) : Ω (sim.)
* : 1
if a : A and b : B, then (a, b) : A × B
if t : A × B, then π₁ t : A, π₂ t : B
if t(x) : B, where x : A, then λx : A. t : A → B such that x is now bound
if s : A → B and t : A, then s t : B
if a : A and α : \mathcal {P} A, then a ∈ α : Ω
if ϕ(x) : Ω, where by this notation we mean ϕ may contain the free variable x : A, then \{ x ∈ A | ϕ(x) \} : \mathcal {P} A such that x is now bound
⊤, ⊥ : Ω
if ϕ, ψ : Ω, so are ϕ ∧ ψ, ϕ ∨ ψ, ϕ ⟹ ψ
if ϕ(x) : Ω, where x : A, then ∀x∈A. ϕ(x), ∃x∈A. ϕ(x) : Ω such that x is now bound
We generally conflate an n-ary function symbol with a unary function symbol from the product type, with a constant symbol of function type, but keep in mind the existence of this difference.

The formulas are simply the terms of type Ω. Note that we actually cannot separately define terms and formulas, since the comprehension term depends on a formula, and formulas are generally over terms.

We could make the formulas a distinct syntactic class as in Sketches of an Elephant: a topos theory compendium, which allows for a more uniform treatment of subsystems, but in the spirit of full-higher-order-ness, we allow for formulas like π₁(⊤, ⊥). Of course, this choice has no significant effect.
Then one would expect:

A language \mathcal {L} is a dependent 3-tuple ⟨ \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {base}} , ⟨ \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {const}} , \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {fun}} ⟩, \mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {rel}} ⟩, where
\mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {base}} is a collection of atomic type symbols (shortened to "base types")
\mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {const}} is a collection of constant term symbols (shortened to "constants"), with type assignment
\mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {fun}} is a collection of function symbols (shortened to "functions"), with type and arity assignment
\mathcal {L} _{ \mathsf {rel}} is a collection of relation symbols (shorted to "relations"), with type and arity assignment

Since the varying names for this logic betray a certain perspective bias, we use the syntax-first name "finite-type intuitionistic predicate logic" here. This is the same logic as discussed in "higher-order intuitionistic logic" v. "topos logic".

This started off as based on Introduction to higher order categorical logic, but I couldn't obviously see why certain types and terms were omitted (TODO: why don't they have → types?), and Sketches of an Elephant: a topos theory compendium instead presents the syntax exactly as we want. (Johnstone has a tendency to explain things in exactly the way one ought to.) The formalization of syntax in the traditional language used Fundamentals of Mathematical Logic 2.1 as a reference (see L (Language)).

I vaguely recall reading that the tradition of isolating the non-logical symbols (constants, functions, relations) of a first order logic for a language \mathcal {L}, and referring to suitable models as \mathcal {L}-structures, was popularized by Carnap, and maybe in particular by The Logical Syntax of Language.
I am unable to track down a source for this now. I'll have to check The Syntax sometime. I can say at least Meaning and Necessity does not make use of this terminology in the same way.
Many authors object to the name "higher-order intuitionistic logic".

Topoi and Computation writes that "Strictly speaking, the phrase 'higher-order intuitionistic' makes little sense, since it is not clear that constructions like the power set are intuitionistically acceptable. What is meant by the phrase is a type theory built on a formally intuitionistic underlying logic." (p. 2).

And Elementary Categories, Elementary Toposes similarly writes "In Part III the first order topos axioms are used to define the higher order internal language. The logic is called 'topos logic' here, although 'intuitionistic logic' is often referred to in the literature. I believe that 'intuitionism' is usually, and rightly, taken to mean Brouwer's epistemology of mathematics, which is unrelated to the origin or content of topos theory. Topos logic strikingly resembles formal intuitionistic logic and the two have interacted, as in van der Hoeven and Moerdijk (1984) or many papers in Fourman et al. (1979). But topos logic coincides with no intuitionistic logic studied before toposes, and this is due to real philosophical differences (see McLarty 1990a)." (p. vii).

Of course this discrepancy is what one should come to expect, since the very notion of a formalized logic of intuitionistic reasoning is at odds with Brouwer's notion of intuitionism, so when one speaks of "intuitionistic logic" it's usually in the purely formal sense.
Combining the two names, I think "higher-order intuitionistic topos logic" is at least a little more descriptive.

The tome, sometimes used at Michigan, but it was never (one of) my course text(s). I haven't used it much for reading either, owing to the large amount of new notation one has to refresh every time you open the book, but it's a solid reference book.
